canberra.title: Police and ASIO brief MPs on personal security measures following Haines attack
canberra.snippet: Federal parliamentarians have been advised to mix up their daily routines and take extra safety precautions following the attack on indep...
canberra.content:
Federal parliamentarians have been advised to change their routines and be situationally aware, following the car ram attack on MP Helen Haines. Photo: Andrew McLaughlin.

Federal parliamentarians have been advised to mix up their daily routines and take extra safety precautions following the attack on independent MP Helen Haines, who remains in hospital after having lost both her legs.

The Australian Federal Police, ASIO and the Home Affairs Department briefed MPs and senators, with the officials telling the politicians to think about regularly changing travel routes and not advertise public appearances.

They were also encouraged to share their diaries with the AFP so police could keep track of public events; and to report more of the threats they receive.

Heightened situational awareness should be employed around their own electorate offices, they were told.

Dr Haines was rammed twice in a carpark near her Wangaratta electorate office by a driver in a LandCruiser on Monday, in what appeared to be a deliberate and targeted attack.

Federal parliamentarians were able to raise their concerns for personal safety during the briefing, but some emerged from the meeting saying they were underwhelmed by what they were told.

Issues of security being provided for homes and offices appears not to have been answered to the satisfaction of many who attended.

Greens leader David Shoebridge said he wasn’t too impressed with the security briefing, adding it was no different to previous ones.

“I haven’t been impressed by the safety briefings … often we get statements such as, you should not tell people in advance where you’re going because that might expose you to a threat,” Senator Shoebridge told ABC news.

“I’ve had that said to me on a number of occasions in safety briefings and I say to the agencies who are putting that forward – whether it’s the AFP or ASIO – I say, how can you suggest that for politicians? Like, that is our job to be out in the community.”

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said earlier this week that reports of harassing and threatening behaviour against high office holders had risen to 1067 in the past financial year, up from 951 in the previous year.

Minister for Women Katy Gallagher said MPs had been “deeply affected” by the attack on Dr Haines.

She said female politicians were often the target of more violent threats than men, but they remained defiant.

“I can’t pretend that women across the parliament aren’t concerned about this. They are,” Senator Gallagher said.

“But many of them, and all that I’ve spoken to, are quite defiant about it, too.

“We’ve found our place at the table in politics. We now need to make sure that it’s safe and that people are supported to do their job well.”

The Minister also said other people whose employment saw them dealing with the public, such as teachers, healthcare workers and retail assistants, sometimes faced similar threats to those directed towards politicians.

But threats against public officials were skyrocketing.

“These stories are shocking in many ways to the public, but for many MPs … these stories of threats against their person aren’t new,” she said.

“It’s something we’ve been living with at an increasing rate for a couple of years now.”

Governor-General Sam Mostyn also addressed the issue of women being disproportionately targeted with violent threats.

“Like any woman who has stepped up into any position across any part of our society, there is a unique and pernicious form of attack that comes our way,” Ms Mostyn told the ABC.

“I still receive that online. In fact, I was just saddened this morning to see some of the comments on my own Instagram page, in capitals with expletives, once again questioning the very nature of what it is that I do.

“Women across the country know that there are certain things that are reserved for women – that go to our gender and they are often vicious and just despicable.”

Earlier in the week, Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek described how someone had personally slipped a note under the door of her home, telling her they hoped her children “die of painful cancers”.

Anthony Albanese shared on Thursday that about 20 charges had been laid against people who had made direct threats to him.

“I don’t look at the comments [on his own social media accounts] for my own mental health,” the Prime Minister said.

“There has been a normalisation of behaviour that can be very aggressive in a way that wasn’t happening a couple of decades ago.”

canberra.title: ‘Frustration and confusion’: Dickson residents may challenge approval of Tradies development
canberra.snippet: The Dickson Residents Group will weigh its legal options after the $94 million first stage of the Tradies’ Dickson Green developmen...
canberra.content:
The first stage of the Tradies Dickson Green development will deliver 246 units. Images: Stewart Architecture.

The Dickson Residents Group will weigh its legal options after the $94 million first stage of the Tradies’ Dickson Green development got the nod from the Territory Planning Authority.

While the Tradies is yet to assess the conditions attached to the approval, Dickson Residents Group spokesperson Gene McGlynn said “frustration and confusion” summed up the group’s response to the decision.

“The decision itself seems very confusing and has a lot of conditions, which seem like things that should have been sorted out before the approval was given,” he said.

“It seems like trees haven’t been sorted out, traffic hasn’t really been sorted out, a variety of other things, which makes it unclear what the approval really is.

“The Planning Authority is meant to figure out all these issues before granting an approval.”

The TPA approved the development on Poppyfield Street, which will require demolishing the nursery, gym, squash courts and part of the motel. These will make way for two buildings – one six and 13 storeys, and one 13-storeys – and deliver 246 one (68), two (160) and three-bedroom (18) apartments, as well as ground floor commercial units, three basement levels of parking, communal amenities and landscaping.

Overall, the masterplanned precinct will deliver seven buildings of varied design, 645 dwellings, including some townhouses, a new 4400 sqm club and 5000 sqm of commercial space supporting retail, dining and services. It is expected to take seven to 10 years to complete across three stages.

The Tradies said the project represented a significant investment in the area, bringing new housing, businesses and services, publicly accessible green spaces and improved pedestrian connections.

It said the club and the broader masterplan sought to create a more accessible and welcoming precinct, with opportunities for informal recreation, community gathering and improved connections through the site.

The club would continue to operate as part of the redevelopment, serving its members and the broader community

Conditions imposed include resolving traffic issues on Poppyfield and Cowper Street, signing a Canopy Contribution Agreement agreed to by the Conservator of Flora and Fauna and Urban Treescapes, and offsetting tree removals with new plantings.

The proposed re-naturalisation of Sullivans Creek must be delivered in full before work starts on future stages of the masterplan.

The club said the re-naturalisation of Sullivans Creek was an important part of the broader vision for The Green at Dickson, and The Tradies remained committed to this outcome as the redevelopment progresses.

The approved development is part of a larger masterplanned precinct to be built over seven to 10 years.

Mr McGlynn said the Residents Group was not opposed to re-development of the site but believed the proposal was inappropriate due to its scale, building heights above the six-storey limit, traffic and parking impacts and the loss of community facilities such as the squash courts.

“It’s a confusing decision, but it’s also just frustrating that despite what we think are a number of significant flaws of this development, despite more than 200 representations from the community which are raising those sorts of concerns, it still seems to have been approved pretty much as it went forward,” he said.

“We feel the planning system isn’t really responding either to the planning rules, if you will, but also just not responding to community interests, and that’s just a bit frustrating.”

A meeting will be held next Thursday, 29 October, at Daramalan College starting at 6 pm to consider next steps, including a possible ACAT challenge.

The TPA decision said the proposal’s range of levels reduced the impacts of the increased height, and the siting of taller elements also lessened overshadowing of public areas, potential overlooking and visual impacts from public spaces.

The re-naturalisation of the creek and associated replanting of trees mitigated the impacts of tree removal.

The Authority considered the parking sufficient to satisfy the demands of the development.

CED Infrastructure and Development Delivery had no concerns about traffic generation or road capacity.

ACT Sport and Recreation initially did not support the loss of the purpose-built recreational facilities. They asked Tradies to reconsider, but the club detailed a viable mitigation strategy through an alternative provider, as well as the range of recreational facilities The Green development would provide.

The Tradies said it valued its longstanding relationship with the Dickson Squash Club and understood that the removal of the existing courts would be disappointing for its members.

“We have taken practical steps to explore alternative arrangements for squash users in the local area,” it said.

The Tradies said it recognised that redevelopment brings change and respected the right of residents and community groups to express their views and have their concerns heard.

canberra.title: Student allegedly stabbed in the hand at Lanyon High School
canberra.snippet: The Lanyon High School community has been rocked after a Year 8 student was allegedly stabbed this morning (Thursday 22 October). The all...
canberra.content:
22 October 2026

Start the conversation

A student was allegedly stabbed in the hand at Lanyon High School. Photo: Facebook.

The Lanyon High School community has been rocked after a Year 8 student was allegedly stabbed this morning (Thursday 22 October).

The alleged incident was revealed during Question Time, with the Canberra Liberals asking what had happened.

“An incident did occur this morning at Lanyon High School and ACT Policing were called to the school,” Education Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith confirmed.

“The incident did result in a student injury requiring medical support from emergency services.”

The student was taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

The Lanyon High School community was left in the dark for longer than hoped, due to a technological vulnerability.

Ms Stephen-Smith said this meant the central messaging system and parent portal had been temporarily taken offline this morning.

“The message to families was unable to go out in as timely way as we would have hoped,” she said.

“I understand this incident has caused distress … particularly the delay in being able to get in touch with all parents, and I very much understand, sympathise and apologise for that distress.”

Extra communications are expected to be sent to families by 3:30 pm.

ACT Policing confirmed officers were called to the school at 10:30 am.

“A student had allegedly been wounded in the hand by another student,” a statement read.

“The edged weapon allegedly used in the incident has been recovered by police however the alleged offender fled the scene and currently remains outstanding.”

Anyone with information about this incident’s asked to contact Crime Stoppers, quoting P2496908

canberra.title: Australian Signals Directorate hit by critical software security flaw
canberra.snippet: A critical global flaw in PHP, a programming language powering roughly 70 per cent of the world’s websites, has disrupted multiple Austra...
canberra.content:
The Australian Signals Directorate is among several government agencies and private firms whose websites have been affected by a global security flaw. Photo: ASD.

A critical global flaw in PHP, a programming language powering roughly 70 per cent of the world’s websites, has disrupted multiple Australian government and corporate networks, including the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD).

The outage on Wednesday (21 October) at ASD, the nation’s lead cyber defence agency, has intensified fears that hackers are already targeting Australian infrastructure.

The disruption stems from two major PHP vulnerabilities, initially uncovered by an OpenAI tool, which threat actors are believed to be actively exploiting worldwide.

Along with some Australian sites, several government websites in Europe and Asia, as well as a few departments in the United States, went offline Wednesday and Thursday.

“We are aware of an outage that may be affecting government websites, including https://cyber.gov.au,” the ASD said in a statement.

“Organisations and individuals using PHP within their environments should follow advice from the ASD and monitor and review PHP official guidance, and apply security patches as they become available.”

It followed that statement with an updated alert on Thursday: “Patches are now available for two critical PHP vulnerabilities. If your organisation uses PHP, we recommend identifying affected systems, reviewing official PHP guidance and applying appropriate mitigations as soon as possible.”

The ASD has scrambled to fix its own site and says it is aware that several Australian organisations are taking their websites offline as a precautionary step.

Industry and Innovation Minister Tim Ayres insists, however, that no Australian Government websites have been breached, emphasising that artificial intelligence researchers discovered an application flaw.

The minister said the “very good cooperation” with AI researchers stopped the issue from getting out of control.

“This isn’t a breach,” he said.

“This is led by the Australian Signals Directorate on behalf of the Australian Government and cybersecurity agencies around the world working with, in this case, OpenAI, to identify a weakness in these systems.

“In this case, it does demonstrate how important it is to have that under-the-bonnet cooperation with the artificial intelligence frontier models.

“But it does underline that there is a constant battle on the cybersecurity front and Australian government agencies and private sector firms are constantly engaged in toughening up their cybersecurity.”

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor described it as a “big issue” and said that Australia’s embrace of AI technology needs to include cyber defence.

“We need to get access to the frontier models, the latest frontier models for cyber defence purposes,” Mr Taylor said.

“This needs to be an arrangement established at the intergovernmental level with the United States and with the companies, and we need that arrangement in place as soon as possible.

“The best way to defend against the AI-driven cyber attacks is to use AI to defend, and that is incredibly important.

“The government’s been too slow to move on this, and it needs to move quickly.”

Former Labor industry minister Ed Husic said the incident reinforces the need for AI guardrails, which he had pushed for.

He acknowledged that the vulnerability was detected by using AI, but added that AI companies have a wont to push boundaries.

Mr Husic said AI companies might “identify these vulnerabilities because they’ve been doing stuff that they haven’t been permitted to do, and they dress it up as a favour”, but he stressed he wasn’t suggesting that was the case here.

“I don’t catastrophise or evangelise,” he said.

“I think we’ve just got to get the balance right.”

canberra.title: Child abuse offender jailed for ‘abhorrent’ and ‘thoroughly disgusting’ crimes
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to child abuse. The child abuse material police uncovered on Ian Gregory Beale’s phones and co...
canberra.content:
Ian Gregory Beale, 67, has been given a four-year jail sentence. Photo: John Lomnicki.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to child abuse.

The child abuse material police uncovered on Ian Gregory Beale’s phones and computer was so “abhorrent”, the ACT’s top judge said she originally didn’t want to describe it at all when writing his sentence.

However, given his offending was so serious and his complete lack of remorse was so troubling, Chief Justice Lucy McCallum said she felt she had to refer to it in some way.

Beale, a 67-year-old from the Canberra suburb of Gilmore, was hoping he would be spared jail when he faced the ACT Supreme Court on Wednesday (21 October) as his lawyers had asked for him to receive a community-based order.

But he was not in luck, as he was instead sentenced to four years’ jail with a three-year non-parole period.

Chief Justice McCallum said police raided his home in November 2024 and discovered 469 photos and videos of child abuse material across five of his electronic devices, including phones and a computer.

“The nature of the material is highly depraved,” she said.

She said the material depicted an unknown number of children between the ages of about 12 months and 15 years old being sexually assaulted, with some of the abuse being combined with acts of cruelty. The abuse would have caused significant physical pain to the children and resulted in lasting trauma.

In addition, Beale spoke to three people online, including over the social media app Kik, and sent them text or image-based child abuse material.

He understood one of these people to be a 15-year-old girl and sent her graphic descriptions of the way he wanted to abuse her and her 10-year-old sister.

“They are thoroughly disgusting,” Chief Justice McCallum said of these online conversations.

While police were searching his home, Beale told officers he had been hacked a few years beforehand, when trying to explain why the material was on his devices. He also told them the Kik app, on which he had been having the disgusting conversations, was already installed on his computer when he got it.

Even after he pleaded guilty, he told the author of a court report the child abuse material found on his devices was “unsolicited”.

“I’m not persuaded he has shown any contrition whatsoever,” Chief Justice McCallum said.

“It is troubling that he appears to maintain the lie, even after pleading guilty to the offences.”

She said creating child abuse material was considered more serious than consuming it.

“[But] downloading and sharing child abuse material is no less serious than pulling up a chair and watching the abuse live,” she said.

“The appetite for participation in this sordid market is what sustains it.”

Beale was born in NSW and had two sons with his first wife. He married his second wife in 2019 and they remain in a relationship.

He had no prior criminal history and suffers from chronic arthritis.

Beale, who pleaded guilty to three charges related to possessing or transmitting child abuse material, slouched in his seat and stared at the floor during his sentencing.

He will be eligible to be released from custody in October 2029.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call triple zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to police by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

australia.title: ‘Nunchucks’ wielded by agitated man in Hannah Beazley’s office may have been drumsticks, court told
australia.snippet: John Lawrence Smart charged with being armed in a way that may cause fear but Perth lawyer expresses concern for mental health Get our br...
australia.content:
A man accused of making threats while armed with “improvised nunchucks” at a Western Australian MP’s electorate office could have been holding a musical instrument, not a weapon, a court has been told.

John Lawrence Smart appeared on Thursday in the WA magistrates court where his lawyer expressed concern for his mental health. He was not required to enter a plea.

Smart was accused of making verbal threats at the office of state Labor MP Hannah Beazley in the inner-Perth suburb of Victoria Park on Wednesday afternoon.

He was charged on Thursday with being armed in a way that may cause fear, making an unlawful threat and possessing cannabis. Police alleged Smart “made verbal threats while in possession of an improvised martial arts weapon (nunchucks)”.

During the court hearing, the highly agitated 56-year-old held his head in his hands and said he had been a musician for 20 years and he was holding claves.

“People, they don’t understand what I’m going through,” he said from the dock. Smart claimed people had “destroyed” his head.

Prosecutors said Smart entered Beazley’s office physically agitated and screaming, and holding two pieces of wood tied together.

He had a second similar implement attached to his belt, the police prosecutor said.

Smart allegedly demanded to see the politician while raising one of the implements above his head in a threatening manner before leaving the premises.

Smart’s lawyer said he was known to carry percussion sticks in the community and play drums.

The magistrate Heidi Watson suggested to the prosecutor that Smart might have been holding “drumsticks”.

The court heard Smart had previously been involuntarily admitted to hospital with schizophrenia and displayed delusional persecutory beliefs. He believed he had the “devil inside him”.

Watson ordered that Smart remained in custody for further medical assessment.

Beazley earlier said two of her staff were present in the electorate office when Smart allegedly entered.

“It was confronting,” she said in a social media post. “My staff did an amazing job and did everything right.”

No one was injured in the alleged incident, which comes after federal member for Indi Helen Haines was struck by a 4WD vehicle outside her electorate office in northern Victoria on Monday.

That incident sparked a nationwide debate about whether public officials were sufficiently protected from threats against their safety.

The WA premier, Roger Cook, said state parliament had been shocked by both incidents.

“We have got to start to turn the temperature down,” he said.

Cook said discussions were under way about potential upgrades to security measures to protect parliamentarians and their staff.

“Everyone deserves to feel safe at work, at home and in their communities,” he said.

“It’s not OK for people to take out their aggressions, their disagreements on staff in a politician’s office.”

Cook said security measures could be improved at state parliament, but they must be balanced with the need to maintain public access.

The Labor leader said he would support making an allowance available to MPs for security upgrades at their homes.

Beazley is the Labor state minister for local government and the daughter of former federal Labor leader Kim Beazley.

Smart was scheduled to return to the same court next Thursday.

australia.title: Almost every shallow-water coral reef on the planet faces ecosystem collapse by 2075, UN advisors say
australia.snippet: Assessment finds global heating is endangering 96% of coral reefs across 80 countries – a figure scientists say should serve as a ‘wake-u...
australia.content:
Almost every shallow-water coral reef on the planet, including Australia’s Great Barrier Reef, faces a high risk of ecosystem collapse before 2075 because of global heating, according to an assessment by United Nations nature advisers.

About 24% of the planet’s reefs across more than 80 countries are already critically endangered, the assessment said, but when the expected impacts of global heating were added this rose to 96%.

Coral reefs are known as the rainforests of the sea. A quarter of all known marine species are found in and around them and they support hundreds of millions of people with food, as well as protecting shorelines and supporting tourism.

Overfishing, pollution, coastal development and global heating have already caused declines in the ecosystems over the past 50 years, measured by the loss of live coral as well as changes in fish populations, the assessment said.

But the scientists said while the prognosis was dire, the findings should serve as a “wake-up call” because reefs could survive with rapid cuts to fossil fuel use and strong conservation action at local levels.

  • Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter

“The risk is real and very concerning,” said Dr Mishal Gudka, research director at CORDIO (Coral Reef Degradation in the Indian Ocean) East Africa and the scientific lead for the assessment.

“We stand to lose one of the most valuable ecosystems we have – the impacts of which will affect millions of people around the world.”

The assessment analysed the current status and future threat levels of 127 coral reef regions and was coordinated by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), an international group that advises the United Nations.

The assessment assumed greenhouse gas emissions – mainly from burning fossil fuels – would follow a “middle-of-the-road” pathway, causing about 2.7C of global heating by the end of the century when compared with temperatures before the Industrial Revolution.

Current climate policies and targets adopted by countries around the world are likely to cause about 2.6C of global heating, one assessment finds.

The share of coral eco-regions considered critically endangered would likely be even higher, the IUCN said, but four regions did not have enough data to assess them and the coral reefs of the western Galápagos had already collapsed.

The critically endangered classification meant an “extremely high risk” of ecosystem collapse before 2075.

The group considers a coral reef ecosystem to have collapsed if the reef could not maintain itself because of a near or complete loss of living reef-building corals.

The assessment did not fully account for the impacts of the fourth global mass bleaching event from early 2023 to mid-2025 – the most widespread global mass bleaching event on record, the US government’s Coral Reef Watch has confirmed.

That global event was bookended by the worst mass bleaching event on record for reefs in Western Australia where a heatwave killed corals across 1,500 kilometres (930 miles).

Marine heatwaves can cause corals to separate from the symbiotic algae that provides them with colour and nutrient. While not always deadly, bleaching can weaken corals and make them more susceptible to disease.

Gudka said the results were a “wake-up call” and were “alarming, but certainly not hopeless”.

He said: “They should be seen as a call to action – an early warning sign before the worst outcomes eventuate.”

Dr Grethel Aguilar, the director general of the IUCN, said: “It is not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover, but it requires decisive action to tackle climate change and halt further ocean warming.

“We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them.”

Four of Australia’s 17 reef regions were considered critically endangered. Five were endangered and five more were classed as vulnerable.

But all 17 regions, including the Great Barrier Reef, were critically endangered once the expected impacts of climate change were accounted for.

Dr Ben Fitzpatrick of the University of Western Australia Oceans Institute led the Australian assessment. He said even after accounting for the ability of some corals to adapt to warmer water, the rising heat “overwhelmed everything”.

“Reefs are like Picasso paintings underwater,” he said. “They have all these wonderful inhabitants in their millions. You can spend a lifetime trying to understand how all these weird critters go about their daily lives.

“To think we might lose that is devastating. There’s one message. We have to stop burning fossil fuels.”

australia.title: Economy set to worsen, with higher unemployment and weaker growth on the way, Jim Chalmers reveals
australia.snippet: Treasury is revising all the numbers for the mid-year update as economists warn of a difficult six months ahead Get our new political ema...
australia.content:
Jim Chalmers has revealed December’s mid-year budget update will project weaker growth and higher unemployment, as economists warn of a difficult six months ahead for the Australian economy.

Two days after a senior Reserve Bank official foreshadowed the potential for another interest rate hike in under two weeks’ time, the treasurer in a speech on Friday morning will say “higher inflation is putting people under pressure, tighter monetary policy is weighing on domestic activity, and we can see that in the softening of the labour market”.

“Treasury is in the process of revising all the numbers for the mid-year update,” Chalmers will say, according to speech extracts seen by Guardian Australia.

“Higher interest rates and higher inflation are likely to mean softer growth and slightly higher unemployment.”

With the Albanese government already suffering the fallout from its ambitious tax reforms, the deteriorating economic situation will be a further blow to Labor and Chalmers’ popularity into the new year.

Australian households are deeply pessimistic about the outlook, and Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, said “things have to get worse before they get better”.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Jobs data last week showed unemployment reached 4.7% in September, the highest in nearly five years. Despite this, financial markets on Thursday lifted the probability of a Melbourne Cup day rate hike to nearly 60%, according to ANZ.

Kearns said the full impact of this year’s four interest rate hikes were yet to fully flow through to the economy – and that was before the prospect of a fifth.

“The unemployment rate will increase further from here, and we are yet to see the full decline in housing prices, so they are two pretty high-profile things that will impact how people feel about the economy,” he said.

“We could be seeing unemployment at 5%, and that will be a difficult threshold for the government.”

ANZ economists on Thursday said they now expected capital city home prices to eventually fall by 13.5% – a record peak-to-trough fall – before regaining some ground in 2028.

With little end in sight for the Middle East conflict, high fuel costs could also be a pain for motorists through the festive season and summer holidays.

Sally Auld, NAB’s chief economist, agreed that “the next six to nine months will be pretty challenging”.

“Growth needs to slow. The RBA is facing an inflation challenge that’s worse than they thought it would be as recently as August,” Auld said.

By this time next year, however, the economy should be sailing in smoother waters.

“Hopefully by that point we should have lower inflation than we have today,” Auld said. “That would be a step in the right direction.”

The government will hope for an economic tailwind ahead of the next federal election in 2028.

But Kearns said Chalmers’ policy options were limited for now, as any additional cost-of-living relief threatened to exacerbate the inflation challenge.

“The challenge is that the government has been criticised, and probably fairly, for contributing to inflation through high government spending.

“But if they pull back on government spending to reduce inflation, they will be gonged for contributing to the rise in unemployment.”

australia.title: Snowy Hydro 2.0 has blown out to 12 times its original cost – but the CEO says it ‘could have been worse’
australia.snippet: New projections by the Snowy Hydro company show tunnelling work is now 65% finished, but the completion date has been pushed back to 2029...
australia.content:
The cost of Snowy Hydro 2.0 has blown out to as much as $25bn, with a major reassessment finding the long-delayed renewable energy project will not be completed until the end of the decade.

First touted by the Turnbull government in 2017 with a price tag of $2bn, the cost of the project in the Kosciuszko national park has increased dramatically over time. In 2023 it was revised to almost $13bn, with construction due to completed by the end of 2028.

But new projections by the Snowy Hydro company, released on Thursday night, shows it will now cost at least $22.2bn, with contingency for a further increase to $25bn.

Machine tunnelling is now 65% complete, and major excavations are in their final stages. Work to build the new underground power station is under way, with about 5,000 people at work on the project.

But the project reset shows Snowy 2.0 won’t be completed and fully commissioned until 2029.

The Albanese government plans to announce additional project oversight and financing structures for Snowy 2.0 in coming weeks. Another injection of taxpayer funds is expected, along with possible private financing components.

Beset by challenges – including major delays when a specialist boring machine became bogged and wedged in hard rock – the project’s timeline and extraordinary cost overruns have been blamed on its unique nature, significant risk and technical complexity.

The boring machine, known as Florence, is still not yet at the halfway point of its 15km tunnel work.

Principal contractor, Future Generation Joint Venture (FGJV), also faced “cost estimation challenges”, according to the company.

Since the project was signed off on in late 2018, more detailed technical analysis has been required, while FGJV has missed productivity targets and failed on cost and planning performance. Global price rises for construction equipment, services and staff have all exceeded early estimates.

The project aims to link two existing Snowy reservoirs with tunnels up to 27km long. Once completed, it will be able to generate 2,200 megawatts of power and provide 350,000 megawatt-hours of storage.

Despite the soaring cost and repeatedly delays, Snowy Hydro chief executive, Dennis Barnes, said the situation could have been worse.

“This project is incredibly complex, it is off the charts even for mega projects,” he said.

“The original contract had so many flaws, and the project was stalled. The thing I’m pleased about is that if it wasn’t for the reset, if it wasn’t for the collaborative relationship we now have with the contractor, I think this would have been worse.

“The silver lining is the project is beginning to hit its straps.”

Asked if he was concerned community confidence in Snowy 2.0 was shot, Barnes said the project would provide half the storage capacity needed for renewables in Australia and would help lower electricity prices.

Snowy 2.0 is expected to be the largest source of stored dispatchable energy in the national electricity market, with its functions to include firming intermittent wind and solar generation and absorbing surplus renewable generation during periods of low demand.

It will provide peak-load generation during periods of high demand and boost supply during prolonged periods of low wind and solar output.

Critically, it is designed to reduce extreme wholesale price spikes by adding substantial supply when the market is stressed.

“I’m confident that we can get the message out that the lowest cost system of the future is renewables backed by Snowy pumped hydro, batteries, and gas,” Barnes said.

The energy minister, Chris Bowen, and the finance minister, Katy Gallagher blamed the former Coalition government for the poor design and cost projections, but insist Snowy 2.0 is necessary to strengthen Australia’s national energy grid.

Labor looks set to attempt to place blame for the delays and overruns at the feet of the former energy minister and current opposition leader, Angus Taylor.

“The government remains transparent about the pressures facing this project and securing the best possible outcome for taxpayers, energy consumers and the grid,” they said in a statement.

“Once complete, the pumped hydro expansion of the Snowy Scheme will provide more than half of the total energy storage the grid needs by 2050, strengthening energy security and putting downwards pressure on energy prices.”

australia.title: CCTV of Beau Lamarre-Condon visiting McDonald’s drive-thru in van allegedly used to dispose of bodies shown to jury
australia.snippet: CCTV footage shows the police officer buying fast food, attending hospital, and visiting three separate Bunnings stores in the days after...
australia.content:
Beau Lamarre-Condon ordered food from a McDonald’s drive-thru in a van allegedly used to dispose of two bodies, footage released by the court has shown.

Lamarre-Condon, 31, is accused of fatally shooting Sydney couple, Jesse Baird and Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.

He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

Exhibits newly released by the court showed the officer’s movements in the days after the alleged double murder.

During the early hours of 22 February 2024, Lamarre-Condon is captured by the cameras at McDonald’s Sutton Forest, about 30km from where he would allegedly dispose of Baird and Davies’ bodies.

In the video, he pulls up to the drive-thru in a white van, pays for his order, then moves to the next window where he collects a paper McDonald’s bag and a drink.

It’s the latest footage seen by the jury in Lamarre-Condon’s murder trial, which has been running for five weeks.

Last week, CCTV showing his movements the day after the alleged shootings was played in the NSW supreme court.

He can be seen near Baird’s house carrying a bucket, withdrawing cash from various ATMs, and buying cleaning items from Bunnings Alexandria.

Footage from Cronulla on the evening of 20 February 2024 shows Lamarre-Condon and a friend dining at a sushi train before taking a walk along the esplanade at the beach.

Later that night, the pair stop by Cronulla Bowls Club and the friend points out the skip bins, before Lamarre-Condon returns alone a few hours afterwards.

Bloodied items belonging to Baird and Davies would be found inside the bins the next morning.

Videos from two days after the alleged murders were also played to the jury on Monday, and released late Wednesday.

About 7.30am on 21 February 2024, footage from St Vincent’s hospital in Sydney showed Lamarre-Condon arriving for a minor surgery, the day after he allegedly cleaned up the scene of the crime.

In CCTV from Bunnings Rockdale, Lamarre-Condon can be seen pushing a shopping trolley through the aisles before eventually buying gloves, a shovel, a wheelbarrow, and quick-set concrete, among other items.

Later that afternoon, footage from Bunnings Goulburn – about 150km away – captures the policeman and his friend speaking to a sales assistant and buying an angle grinder and padlock.

Baird and Davies’ bodies would be discovered in nearby Bungonia a few days later.

The defence team claims the two men were accidentally shot when the accused acted in “self-defence”.

Lamarre-Condon then “panicked considerably”, cleaning up the scene and disposing of the bodies, defence lawyer John Stratton SC said.

The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

world.title: Controversial US-backed vaccine trial in African newborns halted
world.snippet: Hepatitis B study in Guinea-Bissau that was to be funded by CDC and that drew global backlash ‘will not move forward’ The US-backed hepat...
world.content:
The US-backed hepatitis B vaccine trial in African newborns that drew global backlash was halted, the lead researcher said on Wednesday.

It was “now clear” that the study “will not move forward in Guinea-Bissau”, Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, a Danish researcher, wrote on LinkedIn, adding, “we were not given the necessary governmental approval.”

The minister of health in Guinea-Bissau, Quinhin Nantote, previously denied that the project would move forward. “This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese last week.

The study was to be funded with $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with another $1.6m from private partners like the Bill Ackman-backed Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.

“The solution is clear here: take the money and vaccinate as many kids as you can,” said Paul Offit, a vaccines expert at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, who sharply criticized the proposed study as unethical.

The government of Guinea-Bissau now has control over the researchers’ vaccines, which they apprehended when they searched the offices of the Bandim Health Project on Monday.

It was vital to support Guinea-Bissau in rolling the immunizations out to all newborns as soon as possible, Offit said. Guinea-Bissau currently plans to offer the universal birth dose in 2028.

The Danish researchers, led by Schaltz-Buchholzer, Christine Stabell Benn and Peter Aaby, hypothesized giving live vaccines, like the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), may have an overall mortality benefit beyond simply preventing illnesses like tuberculosis – but giving another vaccine like hepatitis B alongside it could dampen that effect.

Such a hypothesis was “fanciful” because the hepatitis B vaccine is a single protein among billions encountered by the immune system each day, Offit said.

“There’s no evidence for that, and it doesn’t make biological sense,” he continued. He also added that there was a very clear benefit to giving the vaccine to babies as soon as possible, because of high rates of hepatitis B in the country and the possibility of lifelong illness and death from infection.

The Danish researchers did not respond by press time to questions about the study or to this criticism. The CDC did not respond by press time to questions about whether the funding, which was appropriated through its global health work, would now be used to roll out the vaccine to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO).

“WHO recommends that all infants receive a first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth – preferably within 24 hours – followed by at least two additional doses,” said Tarik Jašarević, a WHO spokesperson. “WHO remains committed to working with national authorities, researchers, and partners to ensure that all newborns – in Guinea‑Bissau and worldwide – receive timely, evidence‑based protection against hepatitis B.”

Those who declined participation in the study would not have received the vaccines – making true informed consent impossible, experts say.

“Imagine you’re a mother. You want to do the best for your child,” said Henrik Støvring, a Danish researcher who has co-published research raising questions about previous research from the Bandim project.

“If they decide to participate in the trial, they have a 50% chance of getting the vaccine for their children. But if they stay out, they have a 0% chance of getting the vaccine. So how can you say that’s a non-coercive informed consent?” Støvring asked.

The proposed trial led to distrust among Bissau-Guineans, who wondered if the vaccine – which has a decades-long record of being safe and effective – was being tested on Africans because it was dangerous, Schaltz-Buchholzer said in his post.

It “should be clear” that both birth vaccination schedules – with or without hepatitis B – are not “dangerous to anyone”, he wrote. There is a clear benefit to giving hepatitis B vaccines at birth, and not doing so can lead to lifelong danger, experts say.

Conducting a study like this “makes the case that there’s something that’s worthy of study, for which they have no evidence”, Offit said.

“We have millions and millions, arguably hundreds of millions, of children in this world who have gotten that vaccine as a birth dose or haven’t. If there was any evidence that this was problematic, you would know this by now,” Offit added. “We eliminated hepatitis B in the United States in children virtually within years of starting that program, so the benefits are clear.”

Schaltz-Buchholzer also cast doubt on the effectiveness and safety of the hepatitis B vaccine at birth, noting that he believes the study was canceled because it challenges “prevailing medical assumptions, such as that HBV0 does not have non-specific effects”. The study, in addition to looking at mortality, would have also examined side-effects such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. Dozens of studies have shown no link between vaccination and autism.

“All newborns should be given a birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine,” Offit said. “Guinea-Bissau is a country that suffers a high incidence of chronic hepatitis B. That country, more than any other country, arguably, needs to launch this program.”

world.title: Severely ill ICE detainees face imminent deportation to unknown African states, advocates say
world.snippet: Flights to third countries where the detainees have no ties are scheduled as early as Wednesday, relatives detail Send us your questions ...
world.content:
Relatives of gravely ill detainees at two Florida immigration jails say authorities are about to deport their loved ones to unknown countries in Africa despite worsening medical conditions.

Flights are scheduled as early as Wednesday, according to the families and the immigration advocacy group the Workers Circle, which has been monitoring conditions and speaking with detainees inside two Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facilities in south Florida.

The group said multiple sick detainees with varying conditions had been targeted for imminent deportation, and learned about the operation only in the last few days.

“I received a call from several detainees letting me know that men were being pulled in to interviews with deportation agents, where they were being informed that because of their medical conditions, Mexico would not be accepting their entry, and they will be sent to Africa,” Arianne Betancourt, the group’s immigrant rights organizer, said at a Tuesday night press conference.

“We know that once they are deported and sent to these third countries, they are not receiving medical care in detention. They have difficulties getting medicine.”

A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson, in a statement to the Guardian late Wednesday, said it was “a false story designed to smear the brave men and women of ICE as they are facing a more than 1,600% increase in assaults against them.

“No sick detainees are being deported. All detainees are medically cleared before travel and leave with any necessary medications.”

The affected detainees are at the Krome North processing center in Miami, which was found to be experiencing severe overcrowding by a government inspector’s report last month, and the Broward transitional center in Pompano Beach. Both facilities are privately run on behalf of ICE.

Anisley Cortés, the wife of Noslén Sendra, a 41-year-old Cuban national, said her husband had been incarcerated since last November, first at the now closed “Alligator Alcatraz” immigration jail, and at Krome since April. She said he has uncontrolled diabetes and acute pancreatitis that resulted in a weeks-long hospital stay earlier this year.

“He lost over 50 pounds. They wouldn’t give him his medication, and they would not give him enough food. It was a nightmare of a time for all of us,” she said. “He is very sick and needs the right healthcare.

“Cuba will not accept him as a deportee, and we now have proof that Mexico will not accept him as a deportee because he is so sick. And so they told him that because he could not be accepted at either of those two countries, ‘Oh well, we’re going to have to send you to Africa.’

“They told him that Mexico would not accept him because he has too many medications that he requires, and so they said, ‘Well, we have to deport you anyway.’ We’re left with the uncertainty of not knowing how he is, or if we’ll see him again.”

Shalyn Fluharty, an immigration rights attorney, said information from the detainees indicated deportation flights were imminent.

“We understand that just this week, within a couple of days, likely Thursday and Friday, there will be two flights going to Africa, in particular to the Central African Republic, and we also believe Burundi,” she said.

Fluharty said previously deported immigrants were shackled at their hands, ankles and waists during lengthy flights, and some who complained were placed in full body wraps with no ability to move.

“This is what we anticipate will be happening this week for these individuals, based upon what we’ve seen in the past,” she said.

“Travel can last sometimes up to 24 hours. What if you’re somebody who has a heart condition? Who has a high risk of stroke? Who is experiencing diabetes and requires regular access to food or insulin? These conditions take your already vulnerable medical state and make them, unfortunately, often life-threatening.”

The DHS statement said Sendra was “a criminal illegal alien from Cuba convicted of fraud, larceny, and property crimes” and “has been consistently cleared and discharged from the hospital following medical evaluation”.

He was ordered removed from the US in September 2015, it said.

“Third country removals are an essential public safety tool that remove the most dangerous criminal illegal aliens from our streets,” the spokesperson said.

“Illegal aliens being sent to a third country receive notice and assurances prior to their removal, and the Department of State is given diplomatic assurances from destination countries that the illegal aliens being removed there will be safe.”

Betancourt said families risked retaliation for their relatives by coming forward. “This is not a single one-off story,” she said.

“The inspector general’s report confirmed that there is a lack of medical care inside of the Krome detention facility. Families have been demanding oversight, and every day they are experiencing real fear to speak up and advocate for their loved ones.”

During two unannounced visits to Krome in May, government inspectors found multiple violations of noncompliance with detention standards, including severe overcrowding. Holding 1,102 detainees in a facility with a maximum capacity of 882, the report said, “jeopardizes the safe and orderly operations within the facility”.

Other listed violations included an inadequate number of operational toilets, sinks and showers, and previous complaints included female detainees made to use toilets in full view of men, and arriving detainees held for more than 24 hours in a bus in the parking lot because of a lack of space.

Advocates say Donald Trump’s sweeping second-term immigration crackdown has caused overcrowding in detention centers nationwide that the DHS has attempted to alleviate by ramping up deportation flights to so-called third countries.

The controversial practice, approved by the US supreme court last month, has seen hundreds of detainees deported to at least a dozen African countries where they have no ties.

A Human Rights Watch report earlier this month found countless examples of abusive treatment during and after the flights, and detainees subjected to persecution, arbitrary incarceration and torture following their arrival.

world.title: Nigeria confirms Ebola case as outbreak spreads into western Africa
world.snippet: Case in Africa’s most populous country was detected in a woman who had travelled from Uganda Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its c...
world.content:
Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the health ministry said.

The woman began showing symptoms on 7 October and was admitted to a hospital in Abuja four days later, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola. It is unclear when she arrived in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country.

The health minister, Muhammad Pate, said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. “We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had,” he said.

Uganda’s ministry of health said the patient had only transited through Uganda and that she is a Nigerian woman who had been on a business trip to Congo’s eastern region. The Nigerian authorities have not disclosed her nationality.

“Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said in a statement. The ministry insisted Uganda has “no confirmed active Ebola cases”.

Nigeria is the latest country to report an Ebola case as the outbreak spreads across the region. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and has since recorded nine infections. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases, but it later declared itself free of the virus.

Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control, said on X that “we are facing an extremely serious threat,” with a fatality rate of nearly 50% of cases.

“This Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting several countries spread across three regions of Africa,” he said.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control said two weeks ago it was stepping up surveillance following the detection of Ebola in Kenya and strengthening the country’s preparedness for a potential outbreak.

“These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of health care workers,” the agency said.

Nigeria established an Ebola taskforce in June after the outbreak in Congo in mid-May.

The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has infected more than 9,500 people and killed more than 4,600 people.

The latest Ebola outbreak is the fastest-spreading on record and is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, the 11,000 people killed in West Africa’s regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, WHO has said.

world.title: RFK Jr’s ‘deities of vaccine research’ raided by police in Guinea-Bissau
world.snippet: Police seize doses of hepatitis B vaccine from people at center of dispute over research on African newborns Controversial vaccine resear...
world.content:
Controversial vaccine researchers who have been praised by Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) secretary, had their offices in Guinea-Bissau raided by judicial police, who seized doses of hepatitis B vaccines, officials said on Facebook.

The researchers have been at the heart of an ongoing dispute over research on African newborns, supported by $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and matched by the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation for a total of $3.2m.

The police search took place on Monday, involving “investigative procedures aimed at clarifying the circumstances related to the said batch of vaccines”, according to the social media post, which was translated from Portuguese. The announcement noted that seizing the immunizations did not point to “irregularities in the quality, safety, or effectiveness of the vaccines”.

The Bandim Health Project recently posted a letter of approval for the trial from Guinea-Bissau’s national ethics committee at the ministry of public health, dated 14 July and signed by the committee’s president, Mouhammed Djicó Ould Ahmed. A Danish research ethics committee, which had to change its rules to consider a clinical trial, also approved the study earlier this month.

Quinhin Nantote, the health minister of Guinea-Bissau’s transitional government, disputed reports that the trial would move forward.

“This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese on Thursday.

The study was redesigned over the summer, but it would still deny hepatitis B vaccines to 7,000 newborns in the first six weeks of life, in a country where about one in five adults have the virus. Hepatitis B kills 15% to 25% of people with chronic infections, causing cancer and liver failure, and newborns are particularly vulnerable – but vaccination within 24 hours of birth is safe and highly effective at preventing illness.

Any study that would deny the vaccine to participants was “unethical and exposes newborns to serious and potentially irreversible harm”, said Tarik Jašarević, a spokesperson for the World Health Organization (WHO), calling hepatitis B vaccination at birth an “essential public health intervention”.

Through its country office in Guinea-Bissau, the WHO and its partners have been advising the ministry of health on the planned introduction of the hepatitis B vaccine and the potential impact of this study, Jašarević added.

The Bandim Health Project was founded by anthropologist Peter Aaby in 1978, and it is now co-led by his wife, Christine Stabell Benn, an epidemiologist.

Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, calling them “the deities of vaccine research” at a recent anti-vaccine conference. He has several times referenced the results of a study they conducted on the diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (DTP), which the same researchers later conducted again and found completely different results. Even so, Kennedy called Aaby a “very famous” researcher on Joe Rogan’s podcast in 2023 and cited his research when he halted US funding to Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance.

Stabell Benn was a member of the hepatitis B working group of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), helping present evidence to the US committee that voted to end the universal birth recommendation before such decisions on vaccines were stayed by a federal judge. Stabell Benn also hosted a podcast with Tracy Beth Høeg, a former top official with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) who said she wanted to end “unnecessary” vaccines.

Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, the lead researcher on the project, did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about the trial and the police search.

The Bandim organization is deeply enmeshed in Guinea-Bissau but has done little to improve the country’s health and research capacities in five decades of operation, according to a report from the non-profit Stand Up for Science (SUFS). The organization is now fundraising to help roll out the vaccines at birth to all newborns in the country.

“Our investigator encountered significant distrust of Bandim by the citizenry of Guinea-Bissau,” said Colette Delawalla, an American health researcher and founder of SUFS. “However, because of the lack of public health infrastructure, Bandim is often the only option in situations where people are desperate to access medical care of any kind.”

The police raid underlines the fact that Guinea-Bissau is a “fragile” nation that experienced a military coup less than a year ago, Delawalla said. The country lacks the stability needed for clinical trials, she added.

“Guinea-Bissau is in the difficult situation of trying to protect their youth, their future, from exploitation by two powerful western nations and they are using what leverage they have to do so,” Delawalla said.

world.title: US grants deportation reprieve to migrants from Ukraine and Sudan
world.snippet: DHS says migrants ‘retain protections’ after temporary protected status was set to expire on Monday Send us your questions about immigrat...
world.content:
More than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan can stay in the United States without immediate risk of deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said, in what amounts to a temporary reprieve after their right to stay in the country was set to expire on Monday.

Temporary protected status was set to end on Monday for about 101,000 Ukrainians and 1,800 Sudanese. But the DHS said an announcement “will be made at the appropriate time”. Until then, the department said in a written statement, Ukrainians and Sudanese in the US covered by those temporary measures “retain protection”. The department did not indicate how long they could stay or when a final announcement would be made on their status.

The DHS did not respond to a question about whether they can keep their work permits, but TPS generally allows people to work while their protections remain in effect.

The decision marks another incident where the Trump administration, which has previously sought to end these temporary protections from deportation and send people back to their home countries, has allowed people covered by the temporary status to stay in the country but without giving any guidance as to how long.

Yuriy Boyechko, CEO of Hope For Ukraine, a non-profit that provides humanitarian aid in Ukraine and helps resettle newcomers in the US, described the government’s announcement as “last-minute patches”.

It is a “bandage that has been placed on a wound that does not solve the real issue,” he said. “It’s time for US to come up with some normal path to permanent residency for all these people,” Boyechko noted. He emphasized that they cannot safely return to Ukraine.

Andrew Arthur, a national-security and immigration expert at the Center for Immigration Studies, a Washington thinktank that favors lower immigration, said the government will eventually decide but faces no deadline. Until then, nothing changes, he said.

“It’s simply going to be an extension until it is a termination,” he said. “It’s beyond cavil that both Sudan and Ukraine are experiencing ongoing armed conflict, and therefore the secretary is well within his authority to continue TPS for each of them.”

The Trump administration has already terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria.

But in a change in practice roughly a month ago, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorians whose TPS was set to expire on 9 September. In that case they also said that they were going to make a decision at the appropriate time and that in the meantime, people from El Salvador could continue to work and live in the US.

Activists and a bipartisan group of lawmakers have been raising the alarm over the upcoming deadline for TPS to expire for Ukrainians, arguing that conditions remain unsafe for them to return home amid the war with Russia.

Ukraine was first designated for TPS in April 2022, following Russia’s full-scale invasion two months earlier. The Biden administration subsequently extended the designation, most recently in January 2025, when the DHS authorized an additional 18 months of protection through October 2026.

The TPS program for Sudan was established in 1997, and since then, successive US administrations have extended it due to the armed conflict and political instability that have plagued the African nation.

Monday’s decision comes two weeks before the midterm elections, when Trump’s hard line immigration policies will face a test at the ballot box.
